t: Ways to Split Array Into Three Subarrays — Sliding Windows over Prefix Sums
o: We must place two cut points so the array splits into three contiguous non-empty pieces — left, mid, right — with sum(left) ≤ sum(mid) ≤ sum(right), and count the placements modulo $10^9+7$. In Example 2 (`nums = [1,2,2,2,5,0]`, total 12) the good splits are [1 | 2 | 2,2,5,0], [1 | 2,2 | 2,5,0] and [1,2 | 2,2 | 5,0] — 3 ways — while Example 3 (`[3,2,1]`) admits none since the lone first element already outweighs the tail. Elements are non-negative, and that is the crucial structural gift: prefix sums form a non-decreasing sequence, so as the first cut i moves right, the interval of legal positions for the second cut j only slides rightward. That monotonicity rules out rescanning: for each i the legal j's form one contiguous range, findable by two binary searches (O(n log n)) or by two pointers that amortize to O(n) — well within reach for n up to $10^5$, unlike the O(n²) enumeration.
k: Prefix sums convert the problem into choosing two indices i < j with pre[i] ≤ pre[j]−pre[i] ≤ total−pre[j].
Non-negative elements make prefix sums sorted, so for each i the legal j's form one contiguous window whose endpoints move only rightward as i grows.
Zero elements are why both boundary conditions are inclusive — splits with left = mid or mid = right still count.

a.n: Approach 1: Enumerate Cuts with Prefix Sums (Brute Force)
a.i: Precompute prefix sums so any segment sum is a subtraction, then try every left cut and scan candidate mid cuts, using monotonicity to skip and stop early. Still quadratic in the worst case (e.g. all-zero arrays), but it validates the exact boundary logic that the faster solutions reuse.
s: Build pre where pre[i] is the sum of nums[0..i].
Fix the left cut i; abandon it entirely once 2·pre[i] exceeds the total, since left sums only grow.
Scan the mid cut j from i+1 to n−2 (right must stay non-empty).
Continue while pre[j] − pre[i] < pre[i]; break once pre[j] − pre[i] > total − pre[j].
Count every surviving (i, j) and return the total modulo 10^9+7.
a.t: O(n²) — for each left cut the mid cut may scan almost the whole remainder (all-zero arrays hit this)

a.n: Approach 2: Binary Search the Mid-Cut Range
a.i: Rewrite the constraints on j as pre[j] ≥ 2·pre[i] and 2·pre[j] ≤ total + pre[i]. Since pre is sorted, each bound is located with a binary search restricted to indices i+1..n−2, and the number of legal mid cuts is simply the distance between the two found positions. This removes the inner scan at the price of two logarithmic searches per left cut.
s: Build the sorted prefix-sum array; let total = pre[n−1].
For each left cut i from 0 to n−3, stop the loop once 2·pre[i] > total.
Compute lo = first index in [i+1, n−2] with pre[index] ≥ 2·pre[i].
Compute hi = first index in [i+1, n−2] with 2·pre[index] > total + pre[i]; the legal count is hi − lo when positive.

c.python:
from itertools import accumulate
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right


class Solution:
    def waysToSplit(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        MOD = 10 ** 9 + 7
        n = len(nums)
        pre = list(accumulate(nums))
        total = pre[-1]
        ans = 0
        for i in range(n - 2):
            if 2 * pre[i] > total:
                break
            lo = bisect_left(pre, 2 * pre[i], i + 1, n - 1)
            hi = bisect_right(pre, (total + pre[i]) // 2, i + 1, n - 1)
            if hi > lo:
                ans += hi - lo
        return ans % MOD

a.t: O(n log n) — two binary searches over the prefix array per left cut

a.n: Approach 3: Two Pointers over Both Cut Ranges
a.i: Both window boundaries are monotone in i — a larger left sum pushes the minimum legal j up and the maximum legal j up as well — so pointers never move backward across the entire run. Maintaining l (first legal mid cut) and r (first illegal position after it) therefore costs linear time overall while using exactly the same inequalities as the binary-search version.
s: Build prefix sums; initialize pointers l = r = 0.
For each left cut i, clamp l up to at least i+1 (mid must be non-empty); stop the sweep once 2·pre[i] exceeds the total.
Advance l while pre[l] < 2·pre[i]; then raise r to at least l.
Advance r while 2·pre[r] ≤ total + pre[i], never passing n−1; add r − l, the size of the legal mid-cut window.
a.t: O(n) — l and r move forward only across all iterations combined

w: Lead with prefix sums and the two-pointer version; binary search is an easier-to-explain intermediate step if you need time to think. Pitfalls: letting j reach n−1 (right would be empty — clamp at n−2), dropping the early exit 2·pre[i] > total (harmless for correctness but wasteful), forgetting the final modulo on large counts, and using 32-bit sums when totals can reach 10^9. Edge cases: all-zeros arrays produce huge counts handled by the modulo; strictly decreasing arrays give 0. Follow-ups: with negative numbers monotonicity dies and each left cut needs its own binary search (or a BIT over prefix values); generalizing to k ordered subarrays leads to DP over cut counts.
